title: Eurojackpot Game Overview and Current Matrix
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Eurojackpot is a transnational European lottery in which a player selects five main numbers from 1 to 50 and two Euro numbers from a separate pool of 1 to 12. A line wins the jackpot only when all five main numbers and both Euro numbers match the numbers drawn. Lower prize tiers pay for partial matches, down to combinations such as two main numbers plus one Euro number.

Draws take place on Tuesdays and Fridays in Helsinki, Finland, in the evening Central European time. The jackpot starts at 10 million euros and grows by rollover when no line matches 5+2, up to a cap of 120 million euros. A standard line costs 2 euros in many participating countries, with local processing fees and tax treatment varying by country.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
main = comb(50, 5)
euro = comb(12, 2)
print("main-number combinations:", main)
print("Euro-number combinations:", euro)
print("total jackpot combinations:", main * euro)
print("matrix: 5 from 50 plus 2 from 12")
demo.expected_output:
main-number combinations: 2118760
Euro-number combinations: 66
total jackpot combinations: 139838160
matrix: 5 from 50 plus 2 from 12

source: Multiple secondary guides reporting the current Eurojackpot format (5/50 + 2/12, Tuesday and Friday draws, 10 million euro minimum, 120 million euro cap); cross-checked across search results 2026-10-26

title: Eurojackpot Jackpot Odds by Exact Computation
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

The jackpot odds for Eurojackpot follow directly from counting combinations. There are C(50,5) ways to choose five main numbers and C(12,2) ways to choose two Euro numbers, and the two choices are independent, so the counts multiply. C(50,5) equals 2,118,760 and C(12,2) equals 66, giving 139,838,160 possible lines and jackpot odds of 1 in 139,838,160 for a single line.

That computed figure matches the published jackpot odds reported for the current game. The agreement between the arithmetic and the published figure is the check a reader can repeat: any source quoting a different jackpot odds figure for the current 5/50 + 2/12 matrix has made an error or is describing an older matrix.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
main = comb(50, 5)
euro = comb(12, 2)
total = main * euro
print("C(50,5) =", main)
print("C(12,2) =", euro)
print("jackpot combinations =", total)
print("published jackpot odds: 1 in 139838160")
print("match:", total == 139838160)
demo.expected_output:
C(50,5) = 2118760
C(12,2) = 66
jackpot combinations = 139838160
published jackpot odds: 1 in 139838160
match: True

source: Published Eurojackpot jackpot odds 1 in 139,838,160, confirmed by exact math.comb computation

title: Eurojackpot All Twelve Prize Tiers and Odds
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Eurojackpot pays across twelve prize tiers, from 5+2 at the top down to 2+1 at the bottom. Each tier odds figure is a hypergeometric count: the number of lines achieving exactly that match pattern divided into the 139,838,160 possible lines. The tier list in match order is 5+2 at 1 in 139,838,160; 5+1 at 1 in 6,991,908; 5+0 at 1 in 3,107,515; 4+2 at 1 in 621,503; 4+1 at 1 in 31,075; 3+2 at 1 in 14,125; 4+0 at 1 in 13,811; 2+2 at 1 in 985; 3+1 at 1 in 706; 3+0 at 1 in 314; 1+2 at 1 in 188; and 2+1 at 1 in 49.

Overall, the chance of winning any prize is about 1 in 32 on a single line under the current matrix, as reported in secondary prize guides. Prize amounts below the jackpot are shares of a prize fund and vary by draw and by country, so no fixed payout table can be stated as universal.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
T = comb(50, 5) * comb(12, 2)
tiers = [(5,2),(5,1),(5,0),(4,2),(4,1),(3,2),(4,0),(2,2),(3,1),(3,0),(1,2),(2,1)]
for k, j in tiers:
    fav = comb(5, k) * comb(45, 5-k) * comb(2, j) * comb(10, 2-j)
    print(f"{k}+{j}: 1 in {round(T / fav)}")
print("total combinations:", T)

source: Published Eurojackpot prize-tier odds table, reproduced exactly by hypergeometric computation

Each Eurojackpot draw produces five main numbers from a pool of 50 and two Euro numbers from a separate pool of 12. Because the Euro numbers come from a separate machine, a number can appear both as a main number and as a Euro number in the same draw, and that overlap is normal rather than an error. Draws are held on Tuesdays and Fridays in Helsinki, Finland, in the evening, with results published by national operators after the draw.

title: Eurojackpot Matrix History and the 2022 Change
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Eurojackpot launched in March 2012 with a 5/50 + 2/8 matrix. In October 2014 the Euro-number pool widened from 8 to 10, and on 25 March 2022 the game changed again: a Tuesday draw was added alongside the Friday draw, the Euro-number pool widened from 10 to 12, and the jackpot cap rose from 90 million euros to 120 million euros. The 2022 change moved jackpot odds from 1 in 95,344,200 under the 2-from-10 matrix to 1 in 139,838,160 under the 2-from-12 matrix.

Matrix history matters for statistics: frequency counts and odds figures from before March 2022 describe a different game, and mixing pre-2022 and post-2022 draws into one frequency table without noting the change produces a misleading picture. Any historical table for Eurojackpot should state which matrix each period used.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
for pool in (8, 10, 12):
    print(f"Euro pool 1-{pool}: jackpot odds 1 in {comb(50,5) * comb(pool,2)}")
print("2022 change: Tuesday draw added; cap 90M -> 120M euros")
demo.expected_output:
Euro pool 1-8: jackpot odds 1 in 59325280
Euro pool 1-10: jackpot odds 1 in 95344200
Euro pool 1-12: jackpot odds 1 in 139838160
2022 change: Tuesday draw added; cap 90M -> 120M euros

source: Eurojackpot history: 2012 launch 2/8, October 2014 2/10, 25 March 2022 2/12 plus Tuesday draw plus cap 90M to 120M euros

title: Eurojackpot Record Jackpots and the 120 Million Euro Cap
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Under the current rules the jackpot cannot exceed 120 million euros. The cap was first reached in July 2022, and a Danish player won the capped 120 million euro jackpot in the draw of Friday 22 July 2022, the first win at the new limit. Before that, a fifteen-player syndicate from Germany won 110 million euros on 20 May 2022, the first jackpot above the old 90 million euro limit after the March 2022 rule change. The previous cap of 90 million euros was first won on 15 May 2015 by a player from the Czech Republic.

When the jackpot sits at the cap and is not won, the money that would have grown it further is diverted to the next prize tier, most commonly the 5+1 tier, rather than increasing the jackpot beyond 120 million euros. There is no forced payout at the cap in the current rules: the jackpot stays at 120 million euros until a 5+2 line wins it.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

title: Eurojackpot Frequency Method on a Simulated Draw Set
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Frequency analysis counts how often each number has appeared in a set of draws. The method is descriptive: it summarizes the past draws in the set, and it says nothing about which numbers are more likely in the next draw, because each draw is an independent random selection from the same pools. A sound frequency table states the draw set, the matrix in force during those draws, and the count for every number, including numbers that never appeared, rather than listing only the top few.

The demo below runs frequency counting on a clearly labeled simulated set of draws, so the mechanics of counting can be checked without any claim about real draw history. Real Eurojackpot draw histories are held by the national operators, and any real frequency table must cite the operator result archive and the date range used.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
import random
from collections import Counter
random.seed(20261026)
counts = Counter()
for _ in range(200):
    counts.update(random.sample(range(1, 51), 5))
print("SIMULATED set: 200 draws, main numbers only")
for n in range(1, 51):
    print(f"number {n}: {counts[n]} appearances")

title: Eurojackpot Hot Numbers Method
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

The hot-numbers method ranks numbers by recent frequency and treats the most frequent numbers as noteworthy. As a descriptive summary of a chosen window, the ranking is computable and checkable. As a guide to future draws, the method has no basis: Eurojackpot draws are independent, the balls carry no memory of past draws, and a number that appeared often in a recent window has exactly the same chance as any other number in the next draw.

The honest use of a hot-numbers table is to describe a past window transparently, with the window length, the matrix, and the full counts stated. The demo below ranks numbers in a labeled simulated set, showing the computation without presenting any number as more likely to appear next.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
import random
from collections import Counter
random.seed(777)
counts = Counter()
for _ in range(100):
    counts.update(random.sample(range(1, 51), 5))
hot = counts.most_common(5)
print("SIMULATED set: 100 draws")
print("five most frequent (descriptive only):")
for n, c in hot:
    print(f"number {n}: {c}")
print("next-draw chance per main number: 5 in 50, for every number alike")

title: Eurojackpot Cold and Overdue Numbers Method
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

The cold-numbers method ranks numbers by absence, and the overdue variant singles out the number that has gone longest without appearing. Both are descriptive summaries of a past window. The common error attached to them is the gambler fallacy: the belief that a long absence makes a number due to appear. In an independent random draw, absence does not change the next-draw probability, which remains five chances in fifty for any given main number and two chances in twelve for any given Euro number.

A responsible overdue table therefore reports the gap in draws alongside the unchanged per-draw probability, and never frames a long gap as a reason to expect an appearance. The demo below computes longest gaps in a labeled simulated set.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

title: Eurojackpot Rollover and Cap Behavior
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

When no line matches 5+2, the jackpot rolls over to the next Tuesday or Friday draw and grows from the prize fund. The jackpot starts at 10 million euros and, under current rules, stops growing at 120 million euros. At the cap, additional prize money that would have raised the jackpot is diverted to the next tier, so capped draws can carry unusually large 5+1 prizes while the jackpot itself stays fixed. The jackpot at the cap is not forced to pay out: it remains at 120 million euros until a 5+2 line wins it.

An earlier rollover rule no longer applies: up to 31 January 2013, a rolldown clause applied after twelve consecutive draws without a jackpot winner, and in February 2013 that clause was replaced by the 90 million euro cap of the time. Historical rollover descriptions must therefore state their era, since the rule changed twice.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
start = 10_000_000
cap = 120_000_000
jackpot = start
print("ILLUSTRATIVE rollover model (fixed increments, not real sales):")
for draw in range(1, 9):
    jackpot = min(cap, jackpot + 9_000_000)
    print(f"draw {draw}: jackpot {jackpot} euros")
print("at cap: further growth diverted to the 5+1 tier")

title: Eurojackpot Expected Value in General Educational Terms
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Expected value is the average return per line if the same game were repeated a very large number of times, computed as the sum over tiers of probability times prize, minus the line cost. A jackpot-only illustration makes the scale plain: at a 2 euro line cost and jackpot odds of 1 in 139,838,160, the jackpot alone would need to reach about 279,676,320 euros for the jackpot contribution alone to equal the line cost, which is above the 120 million euro cap. Lower tiers add expected value, but a full expected-value figure also requires the actual prize-fund shares, the number of winners sharing each tier, and local tax treatment, so no single expected-value number can be quoted without those inputs.

Expected value is an educational average, not a prediction about any single line. Most lines return nothing, and a positive expected value on paper would still leave the overwhelming majority of lines losing, because the average is dominated by a rare large prize.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
cost = 2
odds = comb(50, 5) * comb(12, 2)
breakeven = cost * odds
print("line cost (euros):", cost)
print("jackpot odds: 1 in", odds)
print("jackpot-only break-even jackpot (euros):", breakeven)
print("current cap (euros): 120000000")
print("jackpot alone at cap covers cost:", 120_000_000 >= breakeven)
print("note: lower tiers add value; sharing and tax reduce it; educational only")
demo.expected_output:
line cost (euros): 2
jackpot odds: 1 in 139838160
jackpot-only break-even jackpot (euros): 279676320
current cap (euros): 120000000
jackpot alone at cap covers cost: False
note: lower tiers add value; sharing and tax reduce it; educational only

source: Jackpot odds and 120M cap as cited in the jackpot-odds record; break-even is arithmetic from those figures

title: Eurojackpot Euro Numbers Structure Deep Dive
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

The Euro numbers are the smaller second pool that multiplies the difficulty of the jackpot. Choosing two Euro numbers from twelve gives C(12,2), or 66, combinations, and multiplying the 2,118,760 main-number combinations by 66 gives the 139,838,160 jackpot combinations. Widening the Euro pool from 10 to 12 in 2022 raised the Euro-number combinations from 45 to 66, a factor of about 1.47, which is exactly why jackpot odds moved from 1 in 95,344,200 to 1 in 139,838,160 while the main-number pool stayed at 50.

The separate-pool design also shapes the lower tiers: matching one Euro number is common enough to anchor the smallest tiers, while matching both is rare enough to separate the top two tiers sharply. A player who matches all five main numbers but no Euro number still holds a substantial tier, which is a deliberate consequence of the two-pool structure.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
print("main combinations C(50,5):", comb(50, 5))
for pool in (8, 10, 12):
    print(f"Euro combinations C({pool},2):", comb(pool, 2), "-> jackpot odds 1 in", comb(50, 5) * comb(pool, 2))
print("chance a given Euro number appears in a draw: 2 in 12")
print("chance both of two chosen Euro numbers appear: 1 in 66")
demo.expected_output:

Euro combinations C(8,2): 28 -> jackpot odds 1 in 59325280
Euro combinations C(10,2): 45 -> jackpot odds 1 in 95344200
Euro combinations C(12,2): 66 -> jackpot odds 1 in 139838160

chance both of two chosen Euro numbers appear: 1 in 66

title: Eurojackpot Verification Guide Using Official Sources
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

A Eurojackpot result should be verified against the official lottery source of the country where the line was purchased, since that operator publishes the result for its own players and handles claims. The verification steps are: confirm the draw date and day of week; confirm the matrix in force on that date, since pre-2022 draws used a smaller Euro pool; confirm all seven numbers, main and Euro, separately, since the pools are independent; and confirm the prize tier from the match pattern rather than from a headline jackpot figure.

For odds and rules, the check is arithmetic: recompute C(50,5) times C(12,2) and compare with the published 1 in 139,838,160, and recompute each tier by the hypergeometric count. A guide or table that fails that arithmetic check should not be trusted for other figures either.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
published = 139838160
computed = comb(50, 5) * comb(12, 2)
print("verification step 1: recompute jackpot combinations")
print("computed:", computed)
print("published:", published)
print("PASS" if computed == published else "FAIL")
print("verification step 2: confirm draw date, matrix era, and all seven numbers")
print("verification step 3: confirm tier from match pattern, not headline figure")
demo.expected_output:
verification step 1: recompute jackpot combinations
computed: 139838160
published: 139838160
PASS
verification step 2: confirm draw date, matrix era, and all seven numbers
verification step 3: confirm tier from match pattern, not headline figure

title: Eurojackpot Fallacies Specific to This Game
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Nothing in this edition is presented as an authentic public record.

Several fallacies attach specifically to Eurojackpot. The first is treating a capped jackpot as due to pay out: the cap is a ceiling, not a countdown, and the jackpot at 120 million euros has the same per-draw jackpot probability as at any other level. The second is confusing Eurojackpot with EuroMillions because both use a 5/50 + 2/12 structure and therefore share identical jackpot odds of 1 in 139,838,160; they are separate games with separate draws, caps, and prize funds, and a line in one game has no standing in the other.

The third is reading frequency tables across the 2022 matrix change as if the game had been constant, and the fourth is treating Euro numbers as if they could not repeat a main number in the same draw, when the separate pools expressly allow that overlap. Each of these errors is avoided by stating the matrix era, the game, and the pool structure before interpreting any number.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.

demo.code:
from math import comb
print("fallacy check 1: cap is a ceiling, not a countdown")
print("jackpot probability at cap: 1 in", comb(50, 5) * comb(12, 2))
print("fallacy check 2: Eurojackpot and EuroMillions share matrix and odds, not draws")
print("Eurojackpot jackpot odds:", comb(50, 5) * comb(12, 2))
print("EuroMillions jackpot odds:", comb(50, 5) * comb(12, 2))
print("same odds, separate games: True")
demo.expected_output:
fallacy check 1: cap is a ceiling, not a countdown
jackpot probability at cap: 1 in 139838160
fallacy check 2: Eurojackpot and EuroMillions share matrix and odds, not draws
Eurojackpot jackpot odds: 139838160
EuroMillions jackpot odds: 139838160

title: Eurojackpot Compared with EuroMillions
description:
This Signature edition presents the same topic in a Signature-original arrangement: the verified public facts are cited with source and date, and the worked examples are Signature-original computations or clearly labeled simulated sets. Eurojackpot and EuroMillions share the same draw structure, five numbers from 50 plus two numbers from 12, and therefore the same jackpot odds of 1 in 139,838,160 for a single line. The games differ in scale and rules: EuroMillions draws are also held on Tuesdays and Fridays, its jackpot starts at 17 million euros and can reach a cap of 250 million euros, and it is played across nine countries, while Eurojackpot starts at 10 million euros, caps at 120 million euros, and is played across nineteen countries. EuroMillions calls its second-pool numbers Lucky Stars; Eurojackpot calls them Euro numbers.

Because the matrices match, any comparison of the two games is a comparison of prize funds, caps, ticket prices, and draw organizations, not of jackpot difficulty. A reader comparing the games should compare those quantities directly and should not import one game result history into the other.

Lottery outcomes are random. No method, pattern, or number choice can predict a future draw, and no record in this database presents a predictive method.
